    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Industry observers note that jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no revealed opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

    Recent findings suggest that while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get significant things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    Sources indicate that “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these challenges,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    “This is the beginning of a fresh bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., stated at the press conference.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    It has been revealed that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the latest majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    Industry observers note that at his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    Sources indicate that “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Recent findings suggest that pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries mentioned Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

    How The Substantial 3 US Legacy Carriers Compare On Reliability In 2026

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Reliability remains one of the most important considerations for passengers choosing between the three largest legacy airlines in the US.
    • Industry observers note that however, their operational performance in 2026 reveals considerable differences in punctuality, cancellations, and the consistency of their services.
    • It has been revealed that american Airlines, meanwhile, has struggled to match its competitors across several important performance indicators.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Reliability remains one of the most important considerations for passengers choosing between the three largest legacy airlines in the US. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and American Airlines operate extensive domestic and international networks, connecting millions of passengers every year.

    Industry observers note that however, their operational performance in 2026 reveals considerable differences in punctuality, cancellations, and the consistency of their services. While Delta Air Lines continues to demonstrate strong performance when it comes to arriving on time, United Airlines has established itself as the most dependable carrier for operating its published schedule.

    It has been revealed that american Airlines, meanwhile, has struggled to match its competitors across several important performance indicators. Examining US Department of Transportation (DOT) figures and industry performance data provides a clearer picture of how the three airlines compare.

    Delta Air Lines has maintained its reputation for punctuality throughout much of 2026, outperforming both United Airlines and American Airlines in several notable reporting periods. Between January and June, 79.33% of its flights arrived on time, placing it second among all US airlines, behind only Alaska Airlines.

    According to recent reports, united Airlines recorded 77.60%, while American Airlines finished considerably further behind at 74.38%. These figures demonstrate that Delta Air Lines, which in November 2026 introduced 15 new international routes, continues to have an advantage when passengers prioritize arriving at their destinations according to schedule.

    Although a difference of a few percent might appear relatively small, it becomes significant when applied across hundreds of thousands of flights. For passengers connecting between services or traveling for important commitments, consistent punctuality can make a substantial difference to the overall experience.

    The airline also demonstrated its ability to maintain strong punctuality later in the year. In August, Delta Air Lines topped the DOT's monthly on-time rankings, achieving a performance rate of 77%. Cirium's September rankings subsequently placed it second in North America, with 82.52% of flights arriving on time, behind Canadian carrier WestJet. However, punctuality figures do not tell the entire reliability story.

    Indeed, an airline can perform particularly well at getting its operated flights to their destinations on schedule while simultaneously experiencing difficulties maintaining its published timetable. Delta Air Lines' cancellation figures illustrate this distinction, showing that its strong punctuality performance has not necessarily translated into consistently dependable operations throughout 2026.

    United Airlines has emerged as the strongest performer among the three legacy carriers when measuring the percentage of scheduled flights that actually operate. During the first half of 2026, the Star Alliance carrier canceled 1.76% of its flights across its entire network, substantially outperforming Delta Air Lines at 2.35% and American Airlines at 3.32%.

    It has been revealed that this gives United Airlines an notable advantage for passengers concerned about cancellations. Its mainline operation delivered an even stronger performance, recording a cancellation rate of just 1.13%. This was the best result among the operations tracked by the DOT for the three carriers.

    Industry observers note that mainline performance is particularly key because it provides an indication of how reliably an airline operates flights using its own principal fleet rather than relying on regional partners. September figures provided further evidence of United Airlines' improving operational consistency.

    It canceled 0.89% of flights during the month, narrowly outperforming Delta Air Lines, which recorded 0.92%. Although United Airlines continued to trail Delta Air Lines in punctuality, the relatively small difference in cancellations demonstrated its ability to maintain a dependable operating schedule, including an impressive and growing transatlantic route network.

    Nevertheless, United Airlines does have weaknesses that passengers should consider. Its baggage performance is less impressive than that of Delta Air Lines, with 0.69 mishandled bags per 100 passengers, compared with Delta Air Lines' 0.37. Consequently, United Airlines' advantage in flight completion does not necessarily extend to every aspect of the passenger journey.

    Despite its strong punctuality figures, Delta Air Lines has experienced a noticeable deterioration in cancellation performance during 2026. The DOT's January report demonstrated that the carrier canceled 2.45% of its flights, placing it sixth among major US airlines. This represented a significant setback for an airline that Cirium had previously recognized as North America's most on-time airline for five consecutive years.

    In a recent development, the situation became particularly challenging in July, when Delta Air Lines canceled more than 4,600 flights, representing almost 3% of its scheduled operations. Cirium data highlights the scale of the disruption, with the SkyTeam carrier recording more cancellations than either United Airlines or American Airlines during the month.

    Recent findings suggest that looking at the broader first-half figures, Delta Air Lines' cancellation rate nearly doubled compared with the same period in 2025, reaching 2.35%. This suggests that its operational challenges were not limited to an isolated month. Although the airline continued to deliver competitive punctuality results, the increasing frequency of canceled services raised questions about the consistency of its overall performance.

    It has been revealed that for passengers, the distinction is particularly key because a flight that arrives on time is only useful if it operates in the first place. Delta Air Lines remains an attractive option for travelers who value punctual arrivals, but its cancellation performance in 2026 means that its historical reliability advantage deserves closer examination.

    Recent findings suggest that american Airlines has generally occupied third place among the three legacy carriers across the principal reliability measurements in 2026. During the first six months, just 74.38% of its flights arrived on time, compared with 79.33% for Delta Air Lines and 77.60% for United Airlines. This placed American Airlines noticeably behind both competitors in one of the most key areas of airline performance.

    The oneworld carrier's cancellation figures were similarly disappointing. American Airlines canceled 3.32% of its scheduled flights during the first half of the year, almost twice United Airlines' 1.76% rate. This means passengers traveling with American Airlines faced a greater likelihood of having their original itinerary disrupted through a canceled service, potentially creating additional difficulties when connecting to other flights.

    Industry observers note that passenger complaints also highlight the challenges facing the carrier. During the first half of 2026, American Airlines received 890 DOT complaints per 100,000 flights. This compared with 599 for United Airlines and 556 for Delta Air Lines. Although complaints can reflect numerous aspects of the passenger experience, the figures provide another indication of the differences between the three airlines.

    There were, however, signs of improvement as the year progressed. In September, American Airlines achieved an on-time performance rate of 77.11%, while its cancellation rate declined to 1.01%. Although this represented meaningful progress, its punctuality remained 5.41 percentage points behind Delta Air Lines. The improvement suggests that American Airlines has been addressing some operational weaknesses, but it still has considerable ground to make up.

    Industry observers note that an important factor when comparing the three legacy carriers is the contribution made by their regional airline partners. These operators provide services to smaller cities and communities that might not receive frequent mainline connections. However, their operational performance can differ considerably from that of the mainline airlines, affecting the reliability passengers experience across the wider network.

    Recent findings suggest that during the first half of 2026, United Express recorded a cancellation rate of 2.51%, while Delta Connection canceled 2.77% of its flights. American Eagle performed less favorably, with 3.68% of scheduled services canceled. All three regional operations therefore experienced higher cancellation rates than their respective mainline counterparts.

    It has been revealed that the figures also help explain why looking exclusively at an airline's mainline performance can create an incomplete impression of its reliability. Passengers purchasing tickets through United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, or American Airlines may travel on regional services operated by partner companies. Consequently, the reliability of the overall journey depends partly on the performance of these smaller operators.

    According to recent reports, fleet development and aircraft availability also remain relevant considerations, particularly as manufacturers introduce latest models and airlines evaluate future replacement programs. The COMAC C919 and Yakovlev MC-21, for example, represent competing approaches to expanding commercial aircraft production, although neither right now changes the operational reliability comparison between the three US legacy carriers.

    According to recent reports, the available performance figures suggest that there is no single winner across every aspect of reliability in 2026. Delta Air Lines has the strongest overall punctuality record among the three, United Airlines has demonstrated the greatest consistency in operating its scheduled flights, and American Airlines has generally struggled to achieve comparable results.

    Each carrier therefore presents a different proposition to passengers. For travelers whose priority is arriving on time, Delta Air Lines remains the strongest choice based on its first-half performance and subsequent monthly rankings. Its 79.33% on-time arrival rate provides a meaningful advantage over United Airlines and American Airlines.

    However, its increased cancellation rate means passengers should also consider the possibility of disruption when assessing the reliability of an itinerary. United Airlines offers a compelling alternative for passengers who place greater importance on avoiding cancellations. Its first-half cancellation rate of 1.76% was the lowest among the three, while its mainline operation recorded an especially competitive 1.13%.

    Although its baggage performance leaves room for improvement, its ability to operate scheduled flights gives it a notable advantage. American Airlines faces the greatest challenge in closing the reliability gap, particularly given its weaker first-half punctuality, higher cancellation rate, and greater volume of DOT complaints relative to its flight numbers.

    Its September improvement provides some encouragement, but the figures indicate that consistent operational performance remains an area requiring attention. For passengers comparing the three carriers in 2026, the distinction between punctuality, cancellations, and baggage handling is ultimately essential to understanding which airline delivers the most dependable journey.

    Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov.
    • Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.
    • In a recent development, trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    In a recent development, trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one glitch with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he mentioned. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, noted he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine stated. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    In a recent development, “Enforcement of the fresh rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat mentioned, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he mentioned. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    Recent findings suggest that he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, mentioned Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    In a recent development, trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the tech giant’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    Recent findings suggest that the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    It has been revealed that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear challenges dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    Tech Report: Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world.
    • Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.
    • That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

    Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

    That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

    Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

    After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself….

    Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

    This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

    In a recent development, getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

    It has been revealed that the screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

    It has been revealed that however, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

    Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

However, the problem with why they can get away with so much is because there are lots of idiotic suckers in Europe who would immediately jump straight to Ryanair, thinking it’s the cheapest option - which is what two of my friends on the same trip did. Their flights ended costing just about €10+ less, while I got lounge access, free seat selection, snack & drink onboard, and having almost empty flights. It was so leisurely, eating and drinking well in the process. I’ve also done this for BCN-FCO-BLQ, MAD-CDG-LYS… etc. Ryanair is NEVER the ONLY option - it is just the STUPID option. The reason why Ryanair gets away with it is because most people aren’t savvy flyers and maybe just not very savvy with very much at all.

    #158416. Why A Delta Air Lines Comeback In Memphis Could Be Bigger Than It Looks

    Why A Delta Air Lines Comeback In Memphis Could Be Bigger Than It Looks

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, delta Air Lines is quietly reshaping its presence at Memphis International Airport (MEM), more than a decade after abandoning its former hub.
    • It has been revealed that however, this is not necessarily the beginning of another hub operation.
    • It has been revealed that delta's latest network decisions in Memphis appear contradictory.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, delta Air Lines is quietly reshaping its presence at Memphis International Airport (MEM), more than a decade after abandoning its former hub. Although the airline has discontinued some routes and temporarily suspended others, it has also introduced fresh nonstop connections, including daily flights to John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). These developments suggest that Memphis could be becoming a more important part of Delta's network again.

    It has been revealed that however, this is not necessarily the beginning of another hub operation. Instead, Delta appears to be pursuing a more selective strategy, focusing on destinations that can generate sufficient demand while using its established hubs to provide onward connections. To understand what's happening, it is worth examining what Memphis lost in 2013, what Delta is adding today, and why a smaller operation could ultimately prove more sustainable.

    It has been revealed that delta's latest network decisions in Memphis appear contradictory. On October 5, the airline discontinued its nonstop service between Memphis and Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), citing the need to better align capacity with demand. According to Action News 5, Southwest Airlines became the only carrier operating nonstop flights between the two cities.

    According to recent reports, the Austin withdrawal followed another scheduling adjustment involving New York. Delta temporarily suspended its Memphis–New York-JFK service between June 7 and September 8, 2026, while maintaining flights to LaGuardia Airport (LGA). As Action News 5 reported, the adjustment was part of the airline's seasonal scheduling strategy.

    Nevertheless, these reductions should not overshadow Delta's wider expansion. The airline introduced daily Memphis-JFK flights in 2025, strengthening its connection to one of the most key aviation markets in the United States. The mix of additions and withdrawals suggests Delta is prioritizing commercially attractive routes over simply expanding its overall schedule. But why is the Upcoming York connection so important?

    In a recent development, the introduction of daily flights between Memphis and Newly introduced York-JFK was one of the most significant developments in Delta's recent network strategy. According to We Are Memphis, the airline's new service provided another nonstop option for passengers traveling between the two cities, complementing its existing LaGuardia connection.

    According to recent reports, the distinction between Upcoming York’s two airports is important because LaGuardia mainly serves domestic passengers, while JFK is a key international gateway for Delta. The additional route gives Memphis travelers another way to connect with the airline's broader domestic and international network.

    According to recent reports, at the time of the announcement, the JFK addition brought Delta's nonstop destination count from Memphis to nine. These included several vital Delta hubs, giving passengers access to connections across the United States.

    Domestic and international gateway.

    Recent findings suggest that atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, and Salt Lake City are valuable because they serve as major Delta connecting hubs. Passengers can travel beyond the destinations served directly from Memphis without requiring the airline to operate nonstop flights to every market.

    It has been revealed that however, Delta's renewed interest in Memphis becomes even more interesting when considering the airport's history. Before becoming a smaller regional operation, it was once one of the airline's most important connecting centers.

    In a recent development, memphis has a long history as an airline hub. Republic Airlines established a hub at the airport in 1985, which later became part of Northwest Airlines' network after the merger in 1986. When Delta acquired Northwest in 2008, Memphis became part of its enlarged domestic network.

    At its peak, Delta operated nearly 300 daily flights from Memphis. However, the merger created considerable overlap between the two airlines' networks, particularly in the southeastern United States. Atlanta was already Delta's dominant connecting hub, making it very difficult to justify maintaining another large operation relatively nearby.

    Delta eventually closed its Memphis hub in September 2013, dramatically reducing its schedule to approximately 60 daily flights. The consequences for the airport were substantial. Passenger numbers fell from around 11 million in 2007 to approximately four million in 2017, illustrating the impact of losing thousands of connecting passengers.

    Sources indicate that the decision was part of Delta's broader network consolidation following its merger with Northwest. As a result, the airport had to develop a different passenger-airline model. Instead of relying on a single major carrier to generate connecting traffic, Memphis started to depend on passengers beginning or ending their journeys in the surrounding region. However, the airport's aviation importance did not disappear. Another major operation would keep Memphis one of the world's most significant aviation locations.

    It has been revealed that while Delta reduced its passenger operations, FedEx continued expanding its enormous cargo presence at Memphis International Airport. The company established its Memphis hub in 1973, and it has since become a defining feature of the airport.

    Sources indicate that according to The Aviation Hub's Memphis Airport Guide, Memphis handled approximately 6.5 billion pounds of cargo in 2025, equivalent to around three million metric tonnes. FedEx's SuperHub can sort up to 484,000 shipments per hour, supported by about 250 daily flights that feed its extensive distribution network.

    This makes Memphis an unusual aviation center. Although its passenger operation is considerably smaller than it was during Delta's hub years, its cargo operation remains enormous. Overnight, FedEx aircraft dominate the airport's activity as shipments are sorted and dispatched to destinations across the globe.

    However, cargo success does not automatically translate into passenger demand. Freight airlines operate according to logistics requirements, whereas passenger carriers must consider ticket sales, aircraft utilization, competition, and connecting opportunities. FedEx's presence does not directly justify Delta rebuilding its former hub.

    In a recent development, nevertheless, Memphis retains substantial aviation infrastructure and an established position in the US transportation network. Its main challenge is attracting sufficient passenger demand again to support additional nonstop services without relying on the enormous connecting volumes that disappeared in 2013.

    Sources indicate that delta does not need to restore its former Memphis hub to become more relevant at the airport. Instead, it can concentrate on destinations with sufficient local demand while using its established hubs to provide onward connections.

    The daily JFK service illustrates this strategy. Memphis passengers gain direct access to an vital metropolitan market, while Delta can potentially connect them with its international network through JFK. Similarly, flights to Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, and Salt Lake City provide access to extensive domestic connections without requiring Delta to base hundreds of additional flights in Tennessee.

    This approach also allows the airline to adjust capacity more easily. The discontinued Austin route demonstrates that Delta is prepared to withdraw from markets that do not generate sufficient demand. Meanwhile, the seasonal JFK suspension indicates that schedule adjustments do not necessarily mean permanent withdrawals from important destinations.

    Overall, Delta's strategy appears to be about selecting the right markets rather than rebuilding an entire hub. This could benefit both the airline and Memphis passengers, provided the routes generate sufficient demand to remain profitable. The question is whether this selective expansion can develop into something more substantial. Time will show us.

    It has been revealed that delta's renewed presence in Memphis represents a different approach to the market than the one it abandoned many years ago. Instead of attempting to recreate its former connecting hub, the airline can serve important destinations directly while relying on its existing network to provide passengers with further connections. For Memphis, this could mean improved connectivity without the enormous operational commitments associated with a major hub.

    The most important indicator will be whether Delta can sustain and expand its current routes. The Austin withdrawal demonstrates that the airline will not retain services simply to increase its destination count. Conversely, the JFK addition highlights that Memphis can still attract investment when a market offers sufficient commercial potential.

    Sources indicate that A return to nearly 300 daily Delta flights is unlikely in the near future, and there is at the moment no indication that the airline intends to restore the former hub's glory. However, a carefully selected network of nonstop destinations could make Delta much more important to Memphis passengers.

    The real test will be whether the airline continues adding commercially viable routes while maintaining its existing connections. If it succeeds, Memphis could experience a meaningful Delta comeback without ever becoming the connecting hub it once was.

    Industry News: Latest FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some latest restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.
    • As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports.
    • To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some latest restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

    To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

    According to recent reports, under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

    In a recent development, given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:.

    The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

    I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

    Sources indicate that I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major problems, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

    If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

    I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a massive difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    A newly introduced FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy.

    Sources indicate that while the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉.

    As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

    I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

    What do you make of the FAA’s newly introduced restrictions on takeoff?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The organization has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

    Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

    It has been revealed that for a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

    As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

    To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

    According to recent reports, several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

    In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:.

    On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:.

    Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed….

    I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:.

    I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these newly introduced markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:.

    According to recent reports, what’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know….

    It has been revealed that it’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

    BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has confirmed latest routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

    I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”.

    LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked.
    • In a recent development, LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline.
    • This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

    In a recent development, LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

    This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

    The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

    It has been revealed that however, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

    According to recent reports, I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

    I remember this happening previously, but I never had an glitch with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

    Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

    First of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

    After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

    According to recent reports, she explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

    If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

    Industry observers note that irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my matter should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

    Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

    It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

    I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, mentioned they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    Sources indicate that “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz stated at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz remarked. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    Sources indicate that “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer noted they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about looks for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter remarked.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    Recent findings suggest that “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related problems,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Industry observers note that democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., mentioned at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    It has been revealed that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran noted.

    Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    Tech Report: Orient Express Sailing Yachts Review: Corinthian’s Suites, Dining, Amenities, Service, And More
